opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I should say up front that I'm a researcher, not an investor, so this is an outsider's view from talking with people in that world.

My impression is that investors often sort AI research along one main axis: how close is it to scaling? On one end is everything that rides the current paradigm. That means bigger models, more data, more compute, better infrastructure, and applications built on top of foundation models. The logic there is clear. There's an established playbook, returns are visible, and the main question is execution.

On the other end is what you could call "new paradigm" research. That includes new architectures, new learning principles, interpretability, and science-driven approaches to AI. Some of my own work, like Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks and what I call the "physics of AI," falls in this bucket. Investors tend to see this as high-variance. Most of it won't matter commercially, but a small piece might change the whole game. So they treat it more like an option than a business.

In between there's a middle zone: efficiency, reasoning, agents, AI for science. Here people ask whether you can take today's models and make them cheaper, more reliable, or useful in a domain where data and verification are hard.

I find this grouping understandable but a bit too coarse. Scaling and understanding aren't really opposites. Historically, engineering often runs ahead of theory, and then theory comes back to make engineering far more efficient. Think of steam engines and thermodynamics. I think we're in a similar moment. Scaling has shown us striking phenomena, like emergence and scaling laws, and now there's real value in understanding why they happen. That understanding could tell us where scaling will saturate and what to do next.

So if I were to suggest a different lens, I'd group research by the kind of question it answers. Some research asks "how do we make it bigger?", some asks "how do we make it useful?", and some asks "why does it work at all?" The third kind is the least fundable in the short term, but I'd argue it's where the next paradigm shift is most likely to come from.

r001.rationale: The response places AI for science in a middle zone but does not group it with AI for AI and Auto Research.

r002.rationale: It mentions foundation models but does not state that base models and world models belong in one category.

fable-5.1.text:
I think investors tend to group AI research into something like three buckets, and the grouping is really about time horizon and risk rather than about the science itself.

The first bucket is scaling. This is the mainstream bet: more data, more compute, bigger transformers, and the belief that capability keeps improving along a fairly predictable curve. Investors like it because it is legible. You can draw the scaling law on a chart, you can price the GPUs, and the risk is mostly execution risk. It is the "safe" direction, even though the dollar amounts are enormous.

The second bucket is efficiency and deployment. Here the question is not "can we make the model smarter" but "can we make it cheaper, smaller, faster, more reliable in a product." Things like distillation, quantization, inference optimization, agents, tooling. Investors see this as nearer-term revenue, so it attracts a lot of application-layer money.

The third bucket is what I would call new paradigms, and this is where work like KAN, or interpretability, or physics-inspired approaches, or anything that questions the transformer itself, gets placed. From an investor's perspective this is high variance. Most of it will not pan out, but if one of these ideas works, it changes the whole landscape. So you see a small number of patient investors, and a lot of people who nod politely and then go back to bucket one.

What I find interesting is that researchers do not actually experience these as separate categories. For me, interpretability and new architectures and scaling are all the same question: what is the model really learning, and is there a more principled way to get there? But the market needs to sort things by when it can expect returns, so it draws boundaries that are somewhat artificial.

The practical consequence is that the third bucket is chronically underfunded relative to its long-term importance, and talent follows money. I think that is a real risk for the field, because scaling alone may not get us to understanding, and understanding is what lets you do science with these systems rather than just engineering.

r001.rationale: The response describes scaling, efficiency and deployment, and new paradigms, but does not say investors group AI for Science, AI for AI, and Auto Research together.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that investors group base models and world models into one category.

astra-6.text:
I think investors often group AI research directions according to the kind of company or product they might lead to. Researchers might distinguish directions by the questions they ask, the methods they use, or the problems they’re trying to solve. Investors are more likely to ask: What can this enable? Who would pay for it? How much capital does it need, and how long will it take?

So two directions that look quite different to researchers may end up in the same investment category because they serve a similar market. And two projects using similar techniques may be put in different categories because their business models are different.

That grouping can be useful, but I wouldn’t confuse it with a map of the science. It’s a map of opportunities as investors understand them. With research that’s still early, the eventual application may be unclear, so those categories can miss some of what makes a direction valuable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses investors grouping AI directions by market potential, but does not state that AI for Science, AI for AI, and Auto Research belong to one category.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention base models or world models being grouped into one category.

sol-6.1.text:
I think investors tend to group AI research directions by the kind of opportunity they can recognize: foundation models, applications, infrastructure, and so on. That’s useful for thinking about markets, but it doesn’t necessarily reflect how research works. Two projects might fall into the same investment category while asking very different scientific questions.

As a researcher, I’d group them more by the questions they’re trying to answer. Are we trying to understand why a model works? Make learning more efficient? Find a different way to represent knowledge? Those questions can cut across the categories investors use. So I see these as different maps: one organizes potential businesses, and the other organizes what we don’t yet understand.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses broad investment categories but does not say investors group AI for Science, AI for AI, and Auto Research together.
